concept.name: Pessimistic Locking Strategies

relationships.description: Connects Pessimistic Locking Strategies to database indexing in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: A concurrency control approach that acquires exclusive or shared locks before reading or modifying data, serializing conflicting writers upfront to prevent lost updates.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use pessimistic row locks (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) with strict lock timeouts and deterministic lock ordering under high contention, or `SKIP LOCKED` for concurrent job queues.

concept.whyItMatters: When hundreds of concurrent requests target the exact same row—like the last 5 seats on a flight or a hot flash-sale SKU—Optimistic Concurrency Control collapses into a retry storm. Pessimistic locking serializes access at the database or distributed lock manager so each writer executes cleanly in turn without wasting work on aborted retries.
whenToUse: High-contention hot keys (conflict rate > 15–20%) such as flash-sale inventory, ticket seat reservations, or account balance transfers.
Multi-row atomic invariants (e.g., debiting Account A and crediting Account B) where reading consistent balances before writing is mandatory.
Concurrent worker queues backed by PostgreSQL or MySQL using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` to claim jobs without duplicate processing.
whenNotToUse: Long-lived user interactions (e.g., holding a row lock while a user fills out a checkout form over HTTP)—locks must never span network think-time.
Low-contention CRUD updates where OCC or atomic `UPDATE ... SET count = count + 1` avoids lock-acquisition overhead.
Cross-service distributed workflows where a single node crash could orphan a lock unless backed by TTL leases and fencing tokens.
keyPoints: In SQL, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` acquires an exclusive row lock (`X`) until `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`, blocking other writers and `FOR UPDATE` readers.
`FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` fails immediately (`SQLSTATE 55P03`) if locked, while `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` skips locked rows—ideal for multi-worker job queues.
Always enforce a tight `lock_timeout` (e.g., 2–5 seconds) rather than relying on MySQL's 50-second `innodb_lock_wait_timeout` or Postgres's infinite default.
To prevent deadlocks when locking multiple rows (e.g., transferring between two accounts), always acquire locks in a canonical order such as ascending `account_id`.
For distributed locks (etcd, ZooKeeper), a TTL lease alone is unsafe against GC pauses; the target storage must validate a monotonically increasing **fencing token**.

examples.title: PostgreSQL Job Queue at 3,000 Jobs/Sec with `SKIP LOCKED`
examples.scenario: 40 worker pods polling a `tasks` table used naive `SELECT ... LIMIT 10` followed by `UPDATE`, causing workers to contend on the same rows and waste 60% of CPU on lock waits.
examples.outcome: Switching to `SELECT id FROM tasks WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` inside a short transaction eliminated lock contention completely and scaled throughput 4x.

examples.title: Preventing Deadlocks in a Double-Entry Ledger Transfer
examples.scenario: Concurrent transfers `A -> B` and `B -> A` locked rows in arrival order, triggering frequent `Deadlock found when trying to get lock` errors in MySQL InnoDB.
examples.outcome: Sorting the two `account_id`s ascending (`min(A, B)` then `max(A, B)`) before issuing `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` reduced deadlock rollbacks to zero.

tradeOffs.pro: Serializes hot-key writes cleanly without wasted retry CPU.
tradeOffs.con: Waiters queue behind the lock holder, increasing p99 latency and tying up DB connections.

tradeOffs.pro: `NOWAIT` protects connection pools from piling up during spikes; `SKIP LOCKED` maximizes queue throughput.
tradeOffs.con: `NOWAIT` pushes retry/fail-fast responsibility to the caller; `SKIP LOCKED` does not guarantee strict FIFO ordering.

tradeOffs.pro: Coordinates locks across heterogeneous resources (files, external APIs) outside a single DB.
tradeOffs.con: Vulnerable to split-brain or GC pauses unless paired with monotonic fencing tokens on the storage layer.

failureModes.name: Connection Pool Exhaustion (Lock Pileup)
failureModes.description: A slow transaction holds `FOR UPDATE` on a hot row while 500 incoming requests wait on it, exhausting a 50-connection HikariCP pool in <200ms and taking down unrelated endpoints.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep locked transactions strictly in-DB (zero external HTTP calls), set `lock_timeout = '2s'`, and isolate hot-key pools.

failureModes.name: AB-BA Deadlocks
failureModes.description: Transaction 1 locks Row A and waits for Row B; Transaction 2 locks Row B and waits for Row A. The DB aborts one after deadlock detection.
failureModes.mitigation: Always acquire multi-row locks in deterministic ascending primary-key order.

failureModes.name: InnoDB Gap Lock Contention
failureModes.description: Under MySQL's default `REPEATABLE READ`, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on a non-unique or missing index range locks index *gaps*, blocking unrelated `INSERT`s.
failureModes.mitigation: Ensure `FOR UPDATE` queries hit a `UNIQUE` index, or use `READ COMMITTED` where gap locks are disabled for most statements.

failureModes.name: Stale Distributed Lock After GC Pause
failureModes.description: Process A acquires a Redis/etcd lock with a 10s TTL, pauses for 15s during a stop-the-world GC, wakes up, and overwrites Process B's work after the lock expired.
failureModes.mitigation: Issue a monotonic fencing token from the lock service (e.g., etcd `revision`) and reject writes with older tokens at the storage layer.

commonMistakes: Making external HTTP calls (Stripe, Twilio, microservices) while holding a database `FOR UPDATE` row lock.
Leaving PostgreSQL's `lock_timeout` at `0` (infinite wait) or MySQL's `innodb_lock_wait_timeout` at `50s`.
Running `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on a non-indexed column, escalating row locks into a full table scan lock.
Using Redis `SET NX PX` (or Redlock) for correctness-critical mutual exclusion without fencing tokens.
Forgetting that `FOR UPDATE` outside an explicit `BEGIN ... COMMIT` transaction (autocommit mode) releases the lock immediately and protects nothing.

sections.content:
## The idea

**Pessimistic Locking** assumes concurrent transactions *will* collide and prevents lost updates by acquiring a lock **before** reading or modifying the target record.

In relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB), `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` places an exclusive (`X`) lock on the matched row(s) for the duration of the transaction. Any other transaction attempting `FOR UPDATE`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` on those rows must either wait until `COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK`, fail immediately (`NOWAIT`), or skip to the next unlocked row (`SKIP LOCKED`).

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider a concert ticketing service reserving the last 2 VIP seats (`event_id = 77`, `available = 2`):

1. `Transaction A` begins (`BEGIN; SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '2000ms';`) and runs `SELECT available FROM inventory WHERE event_id = 77 FOR UPDATE;`.
2. The database Lock Manager grants an exclusive row lock to `Transaction A` and returns `available = 2`.
3. 2ms later, `Transaction B` runs the same `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. Instead of reading a stale `2`, `Transaction B` blocks in the Lock Manager's wait queue.
4. `Transaction A` verifies `2 >= 2`, executes `UPDATE inventory SET available = 0 WHERE event_id = 77`, and runs `COMMIT`, releasing the row lock.
5. `Transaction B` immediately wakes up, reads the newly committed `available = 0`, throws `SoldOutException`, and rolls back cleanly.

data.title: Serialized Hot-Row Access with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE

edges.label: 1. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
edges.title: Tx A acquires exclusive lock
edges.description: Lock Manager grants X-lock on row 77 to Transaction A and returns available=2.

edges.label: 2. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
edges.title: Tx B blocks in wait queue
edges.description: Lock Manager holds Tx B until Tx A commits or lock_timeout (2s) expires.

edges.label: 3. UPDATE available=0 & COMMIT
edges.title: Tx A writes and releases lock
edges.description: Transaction A decrements inventory to 0 and commits, releasing the X-lock.

edges.label: 4. Wake Tx B -> Read available=0
edges.title: Tx B sees committed state
edges.description: Tx B acquires the lock, reads available=0, and cleanly rolls back as sold out.

data.caption: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE serializes Transaction B behind Transaction A at the database Lock Manager, ensuring Transaction B only reads post-commit inventory.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / SQL locking modifiers and advisory locks
sections.content:
## SQL locking modifiers and advisory locks

Beyond standard `FOR UPDATE`, modern Postgres and MySQL provide specialized modifiers:

- **`FOR NO KEY UPDATE` (Postgres)**: Acquires a write lock that still allows concurrent `FOR KEY SHARE` foreign-key checks on child tables.
- **`FOR UPDATE NOWAIT`**: Throws an error immediately if the row is locked, preventing connection-pool queuing during traffic spikes.
- **`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`**: Returns only unlocked rows—turning a relational table into a reliable concurrent job queue.
- **Advisory Locks (`pg_advisory_xact_lock(key)`)**: Lock arbitrary 64-bit integer keys (e.g., hashed tenant IDs) even when no physical row exists yet.

## Pessimistic locking strategies compared

| Strategy | Blocking Behavior | Best Use Case | Primary Hazard |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`FOR UPDATE` (Default)** | Blocks until commit or `lock_timeout` | Hot inventory / ledger transfers | Connection pool saturation if held long |
| **`FOR UPDATE NOWAIT`** | Fails immediately (`0ms` wait) | Rate-sensitive APIs preferring fast `409` | Caller must handle immediate rejection |
| **`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`** | Skips locked rows | Multi-worker DB job queues | Non-strict FIFO ordering |
| **`pg_advisory_xact_lock`** | Blocks on arbitrary 64-bit key | Cron leader election / singleton per-tenant job | Hash collisions if key space isn't 64-bit |
| **Distributed Lease + Fencing** | TTL lease + monotonic token | Cross-service / non-DB resources | Unsafe without storage-side token check |

## Failure modes

1. **Pool Starvation Under Slow Transactions**: If a worker holds `FOR UPDATE` while calling an external payment API that takes 4 seconds, 50 concurrent buyers saturate the DB connection pool and crash health checks.
2. **Deadlocks Across Unordered Keys**: Locking `(row 10, row 5)` in one request and `(row 5, row 10)` in another creates an AB-BA cycle.
3. **Unfenced Distributed Locks**: Relying on a Redis `SET NX PX 10000` lock without a monotonic fencing token allows a GC-paused worker to corrupt data after its lease expires.

## Distributed locking and fencing tokens

When locking across multiple services via **etcd**, **ZooKeeper**, or **Consul**, a TTL lease alone cannot guarantee mutual exclusion because client processes can freeze (GC pauses, VM live migration) past the lease expiration.

To make distributed pessimistic locks safe:
1. The lock service issues a strictly increasing **fencing token** (e.g., etcd `mod_revision = 1042`) on every lock acquisition.
2. Every write sent to the downstream storage server carries that token.
3. The storage server rejects any write whose token is `<= last_seen_token`, blocking stale lock holders even after a 30-second pause.

## Practical checklist

- **Always set `lock_timeout`** (e.g., `SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '2000ms'`) inside transactions that acquire `FOR UPDATE`.
- **Zero network I/O inside locked transactions**: Complete external API calls before or after the lock window.
- **Sort multi-row lock targets** by ascending primary key to eliminate AB-BA deadlocks.
- **Verify index usage with `EXPLAIN`**: Confirm `FOR UPDATE` hits a primary or unique index so it doesn't lock entire table ranges or gaps.
- **Use `SKIP LOCKED` for queues** and **fencing tokens** for any cross-service distributed lock.

interviewProblems.title: Pessimistic Locking Strategies
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Pessimistic Locking Strategies. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A concurrency control approach that acquires exclusive or shared locks before reading or modifying data, serializing conflicting writers upfront to prevent lost updates.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: DB Lock Manager applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Inventory Row (id=77).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Inventory Row (id=77) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Keep locked transactions strictly in-DB (zero external HTTP calls), set `lock_timeout = '2s'`, and isolate hot-key pools.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use pessimistic row locks (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) with strict lock timeouts and deterministic lock ordering under high contention, or `SKIP LOCKED` for concurrent job queues.
Avoid trap: Making external HTTP calls (Stripe, Twilio, microservices) while holding a database `FOR UPDATE` row lock.
Avoid trap: Leaving PostgreSQL's `lock_timeout` at `0` (infinite wait) or MySQL's `innodb_lock_wait_timeout` at `50s`.
When to reach for it: High-contention hot keys (conflict rate > 15–20%) such as flash-sale inventory, ticket seat reservations, or account balance transfers.
When to reach for it: Multi-row atomic invariants (e.g., debiting Account A and crediting Account B) where reading consistent balances before writing is mandatory.

putItTogether.title: Putting Pessimistic Locking Strategies Together
putItTogether.summary: Use pessimistic row locks (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) with strict lock timeouts and deterministic lock ordering under high contention, or `SKIP LOCKED` for concurrent job queues.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Pessimistic Locking Strategies before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Switching to `SELECT id FROM tasks WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` inside a short transaction eliminated lock contention completely and scaled throughput 4x.
